explanations.explanation: That's the one, friend. Jesus says, "…yes, even his own life—he cannot be My disciple." (Luke 14:26) The list starts with the people closest to a person and then lands on the person himself. I'd say that's the part where the crowd stopped chewing and started listening.

Good guess, but a house never shows up on this list. Jesus names family, "…yes, even his own life…" (Luke 14:26). The last item on the list is the person's own life. A house is something you own, but the list is about who you are.

Land makes sense as a guess, since people have held onto their land for ages. But Jesus doesn't name any land here. He lists family and then adds "…yes, even his own life…" (Luke 14:26). Nobody on that road got to settle this with a deed.

Yes, friend. Jesus says, "And whoever does not carry his cross and follow Me cannot be My disciple." (Luke 14:27) Carrying and following go together in that sentence. You can't do one and skip the other.

A staff is a fair guess for people walking in a crowd on the road. But Jesus doesn't say staff. He says a disciple must carry "his cross and follow Me" (Luke 14:27). Nobody leans on this one like a walking stick.

A mat shows up in other Bible stories, so I see where that came from. But here Jesus says whoever does not carry "his cross and follow Me cannot be My disciple." (Luke 14:27) The carrying is tied to the following. I'd say a mat is a lot easier to roll up and tuck under your arm.

That's it, baker. Jesus says the builder will "first sit down and count the cost to see if he has the resources to complete it." (Luke 14:28) Sit down first, then count. I wish I had done that before I tried to stamp a hundred cookies with one bowl of dough.

Picking a spot sounds like a smart first move, I'll give you that. But Jesus says the builder first sits down to "count the cost to see if he has the resources to complete it." (Luke 14:28) The spot isn't mentioned. The question is whether he can finish.

Hiring workers feels like the next logical step, but Jesus never mentions it. He says the builder will "first sit down and count the cost to see if he has the resources to complete it." (Luke 14:28) The counting comes before anything else. Only after that does the building start.
Right, friend. Jesus says, "…everyone who sees it will ridicule him." (Luke 14:29) Everyone who sees it, not just one or two people. A half-built tower can't hide, and that's rough on the builder.

That's a kind thought, and I like it. But Jesus says that "…everyone who sees it will ridicule him." (Luke 14:29) Nobody in His picture grabs a hammer. Everybody just sees the tower and comments on it.

If only! Ignoring him would be a mercy. But Jesus says "…everyone who sees it will ridicule him." (Luke 14:29) Nobody looks away in that picture. The unfinished tower gets noticed, and so does the builder.

Yes, baker. Jesus pictures the king with ten thousand men facing "the one coming against him with twenty thousand." (Luke 14:31) That's two soldiers for every one of his. Sitting down to think first sounds pretty smart to me.

Five thousand would be good news for the king with ten thousand. But the number is twenty thousand. Jesus says the other king is "coming against him with twenty thousand." (Luke 14:31) That's double, and it's why the first king has to sit down and think.

Seven thousand would have the king with ten thousand feeling pretty good. But Jesus says the one coming against him has "twenty thousand." (Luke 14:31) That's twice his army. No wonder he needs to sit down and consider it.

That's right, friend. The king "will send a delegation while the other king is still far off, to ask for terms of peace." (Luke 14:32) He does it while the other king is still far off, not after the armies are in his face. A smart move, and a lot of work for a few cookies.

Battle is what he was headed for, so I get it. But Jesus says he sends a delegation "to ask for terms of peace." (Luke 14:32) The delegation goes out while the other king is still far off. Asking for a battle is not what a delegation does.

Trade is a peaceful word, so you were close in spirit. But Jesus says the delegation goes "to ask for terms of peace." (Luke 14:32) The king isn't looking to do business. He's looking to avoid a fight he can't take on.

True, baker. Jesus says, "In the same way, any one of you who does not give up everything he has cannot be My disciple." (Luke 14:33) He took the builder and the king and tied them straight to the crowd. The crowd heard every word of it.

This one is true, friend. Jesus says, "In the same way, any one of you who does not give up everything he has cannot be My disciple." (Luke 14:33) He brings the builder and the king right back to the crowd. That sentence is the whole point of both pictures.

I can see why that might sound right, but it's the opposite. Jesus says the salt "is fit neither for the soil nor for the manure pile, and it is thrown out." (Luke 14:35) It's not good for either one. Salt that has lost its savor ends up thrown out.

False is right, friend. Jesus says the salt "is fit neither for the soil nor for the manure pile, and it is thrown out." (Luke 14:35) It isn't fit for either place, so it gets thrown out. That's a hard fall for something Jesus just called good.
